chunk_findings.detail: `_hunt` returns the similar ids only when the add-time assessment's action is `"ask"` or `"warn"`, and returns `[]` for every other action. The other action `_dedupe._assess` can return for a match is the strongest one — the "block" case, i.e. a record that `ddflow task add` would refuse outright because it is a duplicate (the `_unavailable` third element exists precisely so that "cannot assess" is signalled separately from "assessed and decided"). With the gate as written, that strongest signal is the one case that is thrown away: for a plan item whose `title`/`body` are an exact match for a live queue item that the plan itself does not re-list, `_assess` yields `found.action == "block"`, the closure returns `[]`, `PC.check(plan, tracked=..., similar=..., known=...)` therefore reports **no** duplicate finding, and `plan check` exits clean. Given intent item 1 ("plan apply … refuse when plan check has findings") that means `ddflow plan apply` will happily file a task that `ddflow task add` would have blocked as a duplicate — the exact failure the duplicate hunt (intent item 3) was supposed to prevent, and it is invisible to the P-gaps acceptance check (intent item 5) because that check only requires "zero findings" on a plan of tasks that `own` already filters out. Concretely: queue contains live task `T` (title "add --json flag to show", body identical), plan file contains a task with the same title/body and a different id; `plan check <file>` prints no duplicate warning and `plan apply <file>` files it. The gate should either not filter on action at all, or include the duplicate/block action alongside `"ask"`/`"warn"`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py `_hunt` (the `found.action not in ("ask", "warn")` gate)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_commit` opens `with log.transaction():`, calls `_file(...)`, and only tests `problem` *after* the `with` block has exited:

```python
    with log.transaction():
        ...
        written, problem = _file(log, st, cfg, plan, pid)
    if problem:
        return O.failed("plan.apply", f"{problem} (filed so far: {', '.join(written)})", **base)
```

Because `_file` returns (it does not raise) when `IT.add_task` reports `not added.ok`, the `with` block exits cleanly and the transaction commits the items already appended, then the command reports failure with "filed so far: …". `_file` itself skips only ids in `PA.live_ids(st)`, and `_clashes` (the pre-flight guard) also filters on live ids, so an id that collides with a non-live queue entry (a done/cancelled item) reaches `IT.add_task`, which is exactly the kind of input that makes `add_task` return not-ok. Concrete case: a plan whose first item files fine and whose second item's id collides with a cancelled queue item — after the run, item 1 exists, item 2 does not, the plan is half-filed, and the operator must clean up (or can never finish at all if the second item's `add_task` failure is deterministic). That is precisely the state deliverable 1 forbids ("atomic: killed mid-way, nothing half-filed"); the code deliberately substitutes "re-run apply to resume" for rollback, and `plan_confirm` will happily release the partial set. To honour the stated contract, the failure must roll back (raise/abort the transaction) or the validation that can make `add_task` fail must be done in `_refusal`/`_commit` before any write.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:_commit (via _file)

chunk_findings.detail: The proposed/blocked transition is skipped whenever `it.state != OPEN`, so a `defined` event carrying `proposed` for a task that is already in a non-OPEN state silently drops the plan link instead of (re)writing `blocked_reason`. Concretely: `plan apply` plan P1 blocks task T with reason `"proposed by plan:P1: ..."`; a subsequent `defined` event for T (re-applying a revised plan P2 that still proposes T, or re-defining a task that was removed and re-added while blocked) hits `_h_defined` with `it.state == BLOCKED`, the `it.state == OPEN` test is false, and `it.blocked_reason` is left as the stale P1 text. `plan confirm P2` can then no longer locate T via the reason it is supposed to key on (the message still tells the operator to run `plan confirm P1`), and if P1 itself is gone the task stays blocked with a plan reference that no longer releases it. The condition should at minimum also cover the already-proposed case (or always overwrite the reason when `proposed` is present), so the plan id is never lost.

chunk_findings.detail: `body_of` decides whether to carry the plan item's `acceptance` field into the body by a substring test on the whole body: `if acc and "acceptance" not in body.lower():`. Any body that happens to contain the word "acceptance" anywhere — not just an existing `ACCEPTANCE:` line — suppresses the merge, so the item is filed with no acceptance line at all. Given `{"title": "add the P-gaps acceptance check", "body": "This task wires up the acceptance check for the P-gaps plan.", "acceptance": "ddflow plan check reports zero findings"}` the function returns the body unchanged; the gate that reads the `ACCEPTANCE:` line then sees nothing, even though the field was present and non-empty. The guard needs to look for the actual `ACCEPTANCE:` line (e.g. `re.search(r"(?im)^\s*acceptance\s*:", body)`), not the bare word. This matters directly for the change's own P-gaps acceptance-check item, whose body will naturally talk about acceptance checks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/plan_apply.py:51

chunk_findings.detail: `_apply_text` depends on two keys the `plan apply` command does not put in its `payload` contract: `hint` (accessed as `d['hint']`, line rendering "to file them, PROPOSED: …") and `findings` (accessed via `d.get("findings", [])`, the supposed "findings of a refused plan" the docstring promises). Concrete scenario: run `ddflow plan apply plan.toml` (the dry run is the default path, `apply=False`). The render reaches `f"to file them, PROPOSED: {d['hint']}"`; because `hint` is not in the declared payload it is not part of the data handed to the render, so the default command fails with `KeyError: 'hint'` instead of printing the dry-run summary. Symmetrically, when `plan check` inside the apply has findings and the plan is refused, the render's `d.get("findings", [])` silently yields `[]` (a `.get` default papers over the same omission), so the operator is shown only `out.reason` and never the findings that caused the refusal — defeating the whole point of `_apply_text` per its own docstring. Fix: add `hint` and `findings` to the apply command's `payload` tuple (mirroring how check declares `findings`).

chunk_findings.detail:
The old test `if acc and "acceptance" not in body.lower()` suppressed the merge whenever the word "acceptance" appeared *anywhere* in the body; the replacement `if acc and not re.search(r"(?im)^\s*acceptance ", body)` only suppresses when a line *starts* (after optional whitespace) with the bare word `acceptance`. That is strictly narrower, so a body that already declares its acceptance with any line prefix now gets a second `ACCEPTANCE:` block appended. Concrete input: a plan item with `acceptance = "run pytest and check exit 0"` and body `"- ACCEPTANCE: exit 0

Do the work."` (or `"## ACCEPTANCE
..."`, `"**ACCEPTANCE:** ..."`, `"1. ACCEPTANCE ..."`). The regex fails to match, `body_of` returns `"- ACCEPTANCE: exit 0

Do the work.

ACCEPTANCE: run pytest and check exit 0"`, and the filed task carries two (possibly conflicting) acceptance declarations, one of which the previous code correctly avoided duplicating. Note this is the opposite failure from the superseded finding (the old code dropped the plan's acceptance on a mere prose mention); the fix removed that false positive but introduced this false negative for non‑line‑leading acceptance markers.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/plan_apply.py:52 (`body_of`)

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to prove atomicity ("so nothing is half filed") but it invokes `run_cli(repo, "plan", "apply", plan)` **without `--apply`**. Per the change's own description, `apply=False` is the default and that path is a dry run: it never writes anything. Therefore the assertion `assert run_cli(repo, "show", "a")[0] != 0` holds trivially, regardless of whether the fix for the previously-confirmed `_commit` defect (items committed before `problem` is inspected) is present or reverted — in a dry run no item can ever be appended, so "a" is absent either way. The test only demonstrates that the *pre-flight* removed-id detection returns code 3; it does not exercise the `--apply` path where the half-filing actually occurs. Concretely: revert the `_file`/`_commit` ordering fix, rerun this test, and it still passes, i.e. it provides no regression coverage for the bug it is named after. Running the same scenario with `--apply` (as `test_an_acceptance_field_is_carried...` does) would make the assertion meaningful. This leaves the fix for finding #2 without an effective regression test, contrary to the hard-constraint expectation in [D-rules-hierarchy] ("ddflow rules are hard constraints (e.g., 'must have regression test')").
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_plan_apply.py::test_a_removed_id_is_refused_up_front_so_nothing_is_half_filed

chunk_findings.detail: `_queue()` documents its `None` return as "the checks that need it are then left out rather than the plan refused", and `_report` honours that for `similar` (`... if queue else None`). But `known` is computed as `_live(queue[2] if queue else None)`, and `_live(None)` returns `[]`. `known` is the live-id universe that `plancheck.check` validates `needs`/references against (that is why `PA.live_ids(st)` is passed at all), so an empty list asserts "no item is live", it does not disable the check. Demonstrated: run `ddflow plan check p.toml` where `_load` raises `OSError`/`ValueError`/`LookupError` (unreadable/absent ddflow state) on a plan whose items declare `needs = ["<already-filed-id>"]` (exactly the shape of the 11 P-gaps tasks the acceptance check builds). `_live` returns `[]`, `PC.check` resolves none of those needs and reports findings, so `plan check` exits non-zero and `plan apply` refuses a plan whose queue checks were supposed to be skipped — the very outcome the comment says must not happen. Passing `known=None` (or having `_live` return `None` when `st is None`) is what "left out" requires, mirroring the `similar` branch.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/plan.py:_report / _live

chunk_findings.detail: The only check that a plan item's `parent` exists in the queue is `_missing_parents`, and it (a) runs once, *before* the log lock is taken, and (b) treats a removed id as present, because it tests `p not in st.items` while `st.items` keeps tombstones — `_clashes` relies on exactly that ("Removed ids too"). The locked re-check in `_commit` then re-validates only `needs` (against `live`, i.e. tombstones excluded): `changed = _clashes(...) + [d for i in plan for d in PA._list(plan[i], "needs") if d not in plan and d not in live]`. So the two reference kinds are validated asymmetrically. Concrete: remove a phase (`PH`), then apply a plan whose task declares `parent: PH`; `_missing_parents` sees `PH in st.items` and reports nothing, `_commit` never looks at `parent`, so the item is written with a dangling parent. Identically, if `PH` is removed by another agent after the pre-check passes, the write still happens — the exact race the docstring promises to close ("Decide again under the log lock, from the log as it is NOW"). A `needs: PH` reference in the same position is refused; a `parent: PH` one is not.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/api/plan.py:_commit` / `_missing_parents`

chunk_findings.detail: `(p := str(it.get("parent", "")))` converts an explicit null to the literal string `"None"`. Input: a plan item written as `parent:` / `parent: null` (or `parent: ~`) in YAML — `.get` returns `None`, not the default `""`, so `p == "None"`, which is truthy, is not a plan id, and is not in `st.items`; the plan is then rejected with `parent not in the plan or the queue: <i> -> None`, even though no parent was declared. The guard was clearly meant to be "if the value is absent/empty, skip"; `str()` before the truthiness test defeats it for `None`.
chunk_findings.title: `ddflow/api/plan.py:_missing_parents`

chunk_findings.detail: Unlike `_commit`, `plan_confirm` takes no log lock around its *decision*: `waiting = PA.proposed_by(st, plan_id)` is computed from the snapshot returned by `_load`, and the `with log.transaction():` block only appends `item.unblocked` for that stale list without re-folding the log or re-checking that each id is still proposed/present. Two operators confirming the same plan concurrently both see the same `waiting` and both emit `item.unblocked` for the same ids (double release), and an id removed between the load and the transaction still receives an `item.unblocked` event. The sibling path in this same change explicitly guards against precisely this ("Decide again under the log lock, from the log as it is NOW", `_commit`), so the operator-only path is the weaker of the two.

chunk_findings.detail:
The proposed-state logic dereferences `blocked_reason` without guarding for a missing value:

    again = it.state == BLOCKED and it.blocked_reason.startswith(PROPOSED_PREFIX)

`blocked_reason` is an optional field whose default is `None` for an item that has no recorded reason (it is only *set* to a string when something explicitly records one — including this very block). If an add/update event carrying `proposed` arrives for a task that is already in the `BLOCKED` state but whose `blocked_reason` is `None` — e.g. a task materialised from a stored/imported definition with `state: blocked` and no `blocked_reason` (the field round-trips as null), or one whose reason was cleared while it stayed blocked — the first conjunct is `True`, so Python evaluates `None.startswith(...)` and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'startswith'`. Because this statement is part of applying the event, the whole add/update transaction for that task aborts instead of leaving the item untouched. Guarding with `(it.blocked_reason or "")` (or `isinstance(it.blocked_reason, str)`) avoids the crash.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/handlers/items.py:98 (the `again` / `it.blocked_reason.startswith(...)` line)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new exemption silences the coherence test for a writer whose input text is *external* (a plan file or stdin), unlike every other entry in this table, whose text is drawn from an already-tracked item (`split` takes the parent's text, `_add_ports` takes ports of a fix `task_add` just checked, `resolve` re-records a rival add). The exemption is justified by the claim that "`plan check` already ran the duplicate hunt over" the plan. That justification only holds if the check invoked on the plan-apply path actually receives the `similar` finder — and the change's own context says that wiring is a *separate, separately-tracked gap*: "the duplicate hunt: inject `services.similar` as `plancheck.check`'s `similar` parameter (the parameter exists and is tested; `api/plan.py` passes nothing for it today)". `similar` is an optional parameter of `plancheck.check`, so a call site that omits it (or a `plan apply --apply` path that only runs the structural checks) will not perform the duplicate hunt at all.

Concrete failure: an existing ready task has body `X`. An operator writes a plan containing a task with body `X` and runs `ddflow plan apply --apply`. If the apply path runs `check` without `similar`, no duplicate finding is produced, `_file` writes the duplicate as a PROPOSED task, and the one test that would otherwise have flagged `api/plan.py:_file` as an unchecked text writer is disabled by this entry — so the regression is invisible in CI. The exemption should be conditional on `check` being invoked with `similar` (or `_file` should itself pass/route through the similar check), rather than asserting a guarantee the change context still lists as missing.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_coherence_coverage.py:177 (`WRITERS_EXEMPT["api/plan.py:_file"]`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new early block is guarded by the exact complement of the guard that follows it, so the added return can never execute. The flow is now: `if waiting and yes and reason.strip(): …` (inside it, `if waiting: return O.ok(...)`); then `if not waiting: return O.nothing("nothing proposed by plan X is waiting")`; then `if not yes or not reason.strip(): return O.refused(...)`; then the new return. Any call that reaches the last statement has `waiting` truthy (otherwise the `if not waiting` branch fired) and `not (yes and reason.strip())` (otherwise the early block would have run and either returned `O.ok` or emptied `waiting`), which is precisely the refused condition — so it is always intercepted by the `O.refused` branch. Concrete case: plan `P` has item `A` in the proposed/blocked state; two clients run `ddflow plan confirm P --yes --reason r` concurrently. The first commits `item.unblocked`; the second re-folds under the lock, sees `waiting == []`, appends nothing, and falls out of the early block into `if not waiting:` — it reports "nothing proposed by plan P is waiting", and the newly added "plan P was confirmed meanwhile" branch (the one evidently written to describe this race, per the `# decided under the lock` comment) is dead code that never runs.

chunk_findings.detail: `unknown_deps` now returns an empty list whenever `known is None`, i.e. whenever the queue could not be read. That is a silent, fail‑open bypass: `plan check`/`plan apply` promise to refuse when the check has findings, but on this path every `needs`/`parent` that resolves to nothing is swallowed instead of reported. Concretely, take the new test `test_a_parent_removed_from_the_queue_is_refused`: it only passes because the queue read succeeds and yields `known=[]`, so `unknown_deps` reports `PH`. Run the identical plan in the environment the new docstring is written for — the queue read raises (corrupted/absent state, permission error, transient store failure) — and `known` is `None`; `unknown_deps` then returns `[]`, the report is clean, and `plan apply` files the item with a dangling `parent`/`needs` instead of refusing, exactly the half-filed/invalid state atomic apply is supposed to prevent. When the queue genuinely cannot be read, the honest outcomes are "refuse" or an explicit finding about the unreadable queue; returning `[]` converts an unverifiable dependency into an accepted one.
